title: The training principles series: noob gains
summary: Defines 'noob gains' as the rapid strength and muscle gains of the first months of lifting, explains why they happen (novel stress makes muscles rebuild bigger), and argues beginners should use that grace period to learn compounds and some isolation to set up their long-term career, since gains later become a game of inches for naturals.

claims.claim: In lifting, 'noob' is a neutral term for a beginner; noob gains are the period at the start when you progress very fast in strength and muscle.
The longer your noob gains last, the better your genetic potential likely is.
It's true that anything works for a beginner, but certain lifts and programs are far more beneficial, both now and for the rest of your lifting career.
Noob gains may represent only 3-4% of all the time you'll spend lifting, so use that grace period to set yourself up for later success.
Beginners should run a compound-based program (not necessarily the big three) and add isolation movements based on what they want their body to look like.
Noob gains last about six months for some people and up to two years for others.
During noob gains you don't need to think hard about nutrition; results come with minimal effort.
Later the relation reverses: more effort yields gains but less and less proportionally, until advanced naturals progress millimetre by millimetre, a 'game of inches'.
Unlike arm wrestling, swimming or running, where beginners improve on a slow curve, bodybuilding gains spike right at the start then taper.
You'll never experience the initial spike again unless you stop being natural, which he doesn't recommend: stay natty.

The body responds fast to lifting because the movements are novel (e.g. you almost never squat to depth in daily life); muscles break down and rebuild bigger and stronger as a defence against future stress.
Over time the breakdown-rebuild process slows, sometimes stagnating, and needs more stimulus; at the start a tiny stimulus is enough to grow a lot.
